title: How Can Great Firms Fail? Insights from the Hard Disk Drive Industry
hook: The firm that failed had just posted its best quarterly numbers, and every decision that led there was sound.
counterintuition: Failure looks like negligence from the outside. Inside, it looks like a very good quarter. In fact, the same discipline that sharpens execution in an established market can narrow what that market is allowed to show you.
tryThisNow: Name one type of buyer who never shows up in your customer feedback. Write down what they use instead of your product. That gap is where the next relevant signal lives.
keyTakeaway: Your current customers define what your business should improve next. That same definition quietly excludes the buyers outside their world, which is where the next market is forming.

breakdown.fastRead:
The product team had a full quarter of customer feedback and every piece of it said the same thing: the current format was exactly right. No major buyer wanted the new one. The performance gap was real, the quality comparison was honest, and the investment case for staying the course was solid. The project was rejected in a meeting that followed good process and reached the wrong conclusion.

Serving your current customers well is not the mistake. It is the mechanism. Resource allocation follows what your best buyers will pay for, which means it also points away from what your best buyers cannot yet use.

What they cannot tell you is where the market is forming that will replace them.
breakdown.deepRead:
The hard disk drive industry ran through product generations so quickly that researchers used it the way biologists use fruit flies: the cycle was short enough to observe complete. Over two decades, market leadership transferred multiple times. Not because the leaders stopped improving. Because they improved exactly what their current buyers wanted.

Each generation brought better capacity, speed, and reliability. The companies that led each generation had earned their position by doing precisely that. The problem emerged when a new form factor appeared that offered worse performance on every dimension the leading customers cared about, but served a market the leaders barely noticed. Smaller drives were cheaper, used less power, and fit into portable computers that enterprise buyers considered peripheral. No data center manager was asking for one. No enterprise account generated a project plan for it. The investment never cleared the resource allocation meeting.

What cleared those meetings was more of what the current customers were already buying. That is not negligence. That is rational resource allocation functioning exactly as designed.

The disk drive market was the closest thing to a controlled lab that business research had found: generations turned fast enough that you could watch a leader vanish in real time. The companies that disappeared were often the most competent operators in the industry. Their customers had simply shaped their line of sight so precisely that the next market was invisible until it was already large.

The mechanism works like this: your budget process is a measuring instrument calibrated to your current customers. Whatever they cannot use does not generate signal. A technology that is unappealing to your top accounts produces zero data on your dashboards: not negative data, not a warning, just silence. Silence gets misread as absence.
breakdown.fullRead:
Think about what a disciplined customer listening process actually produces. A company that surveys its best buyers, tracks their satisfaction, and funds the improvements they request is doing what good management requires. The feedback is real. The investment follows the feedback. The product improves in exactly the ways the customers specified.

What the feedback cannot contain is the preferences of buyers who are not yet in the room. A buyer who has not adopted the category cannot describe what would make it right for them. A market that does not yet have a name cannot fill out a survey. So a well-run feedback process produces a faithful picture of the existing market and a blank page where the next market sits.

Consider what Camille's expansion dashboard showed her. Revenue per location was rising. Renewal rates tracked above baseline. Customer satisfaction held quarter over quarter. Every metric that had predicted success in the previous six markets was pointing in the same direction for the next three. The committee approval was correct given what the dashboard measured. The dashboard was correct given the customers it measured. Each link in the chain was sound, and the chain led somewhere the dashboard could not describe.

You probably have a version of this. Not for a video rental operation. Maybe for a product line, a service tier, or a client segment that generates strong numbers right now. Ask which buyers are generating signal in your measurement system. Then ask which buyers are not. The absent ones are not necessarily the most important buyers for the next decade. They might be. Your measurement system cannot tell you either way.

The usual objection to all of this is that companies cannot chase every possible market and must focus on what generates revenue. That objection is correct, and the argument here is not against it. The argument is not that incumbents should stop serving their profitable customers. It is narrower: a company whose investment decisions are made entirely by signals from profitable customers will systematically miss the opportunities that profitable customers cannot describe. Discipline applied to the present is the right tool for managing the present. Applied as the only tool for assessing the future, it produces a structural blind spot: not a character flaw, not a failure of nerve, but a systematic gap between what the current measurement instruments can reach and what is forming beyond them.

Here is the practical version. Your best customers are giving you the most accurate map of where you already are. The non-customer, the buyer who finds your product too expensive, too complex, or simply irrelevant to their situation, is not a lost prospect. They are the outline of the next network. They cannot tell you what it will look like. They can tell you that it is forming somewhere beyond them.

Good management applied to the current business is the mechanism, not the solution.

A company can have excellent survey methodology, a well-run budget process, a strong performance culture, and a committed leadership team. It can still produce this outcome reliably, repeatedly, across industries and eras. The failure does not require bad decisions. It requires only that the decisions stay inside the frame the current customers define.

examples.title: Charlotte Uses Advertiser Feedback to Shelve the Digital Column

planSpec.domain: newspaper publisher debating whether to expand digital classifieds alongside the print edition
planSpec.audience: a publisher whose print classified revenue still pays most of the salaries
planSpec.stakes: the online classifieds look weak and niche while the print edition still dominates, but the trend line is clear to anyone who looks
planSpec.requiredBeat: Charlotte hears from her best advertisers that the online product is too thin to bother with and uses that feedback to justify not investing more in it rather than to notice that those advertisers are not the ones who will define the next decade

examples.scenario: Charlotte has already set down her coffee when the agency buyer slides the rate card back across the table. "We're not sending any budgets there," he says. The weekly advertiser review is spread in front of her: six pages of print performance data, one narrow column at the far right showing forty-two digital classified listings last week against nine hundred in the same print section. Every significant buyer in the room is a print buyer. Every one of them has said the same thing. Charlotte must decide whether to take their consensus back to the product team as evidence that the digital investment proposal should be shelved.
examples.whatToDo: Ask which advertisers are not in the room and what they are using instead. The buyers at the table are telling you the truth about the current product. They cannot tell you anything about the next buyer base.
examples.whyItMatters: Feedback from current profitable advertisers accurately describes what current profitable advertisers need. It produces no information about the category of buyers forming outside the room who do not yet use your product.

examples.title: James Takes the Franchise Scores to the Investment Committee

planSpec.domain: travel agency chain evaluating whether to integrate an online booking tool its mid-tier franchisees don't want
planSpec.audience: a regional VP whose strongest franchisees are the ones most satisfied with the current model
planSpec.stakes: the strongest franchisees are loud, profitable, and dismissive of online booking — and their dismissal sounds like data
planSpec.requiredBeat: James takes the franchisee satisfaction scores to the investment committee and the online tool is voted down because it doesn't serve the customers who most clearly generate revenue right now

examples.scenario: Performance reports on three-hole paper, fanned across the board table in order of franchise revenue. James checks the top line before the chair sits down. The seven highest-performing franchises are all in the room. None of them use the online booking pilot. All of them have said the same thing about it: their clients call. James is presenting the pilot's twelve-month results to a committee where the franchisees he most relies on have already made clear that the tool does not serve their customers, and their satisfaction scores are the highest in the chain.
examples.whatToDo: Track the customers who are booking through channels the committee never sees. Feedback from top franchisees accurately describes top-franchisee customers and produces a blind spot everywhere else.
examples.whyItMatters: The franchisees who are loudest in the investment committee are the ones who generate the most revenue, so their signal dominates. What goes unmeasured is whether a different type of buyer would use a channel those franchisees have already dismissed.

examples.title: David's Survey Finds No Threat from Digital Cameras

planSpec.domain: film camera manufacturer reviewing quarterly financials as the first consumer digital cameras arrive
planSpec.audience: a product manager whose core market is professional and serious-amateur photographers who actively prefer film
planSpec.stakes: the digital cameras on the market look worse by every measure the product team uses to evaluate cameras — grain, color range, cost per image
planSpec.requiredBeat: David presents the digital camera market analysis and concludes it is not yet a real threat because no professional photographer in their survey finds it acceptable — a conclusion that is technically correct and structurally misleading

examples.scenario: At 9:15 a.m. Thursday, David opens the competitive analysis. The quality comparison matrix covers grain resolution, color saturation, and cost per image. Film wins on all three columns. The professional photographer survey sampled 200 working photographers: none of them would consider digital for client work at current quality levels. The market-entry recommendation on page twelve says hold position. David must decide whether to accept the analysis as written or ask why the survey only sampled professional photographers.
examples.whatToDo: Commission a separate study covering buyers who do not currently use film cameras at all. The survey proved what professional photographers need. It produced no information about what a different category of buyer might accept.
examples.whyItMatters: A survey that samples only the current customer base confirms the current product's position accurately and generates no information about the next buyer base. The recommendation is correct for the audience it surveyed.

examples.title: Camille's Dashboard Approves the Seventh Market

planSpec.domain: video rental chain opening new locations in markets where rental revenue is still growing
planSpec.audience: a strategy director whose expansion model has worked reliably for six years
planSpec.stakes: the expansion signals look solid because the best existing customers are in new markets, even as a different kind of viewing is beginning at the edges
planSpec.requiredBeat: Camille's expansion plan is approved because the metrics it uses are all strong. The metrics that would catch what is happening outside the current value network are not on the dashboard.

examples.scenario: It took Camille three expansion cycles to see what the dashboard had been hiding from her. The prediction model had worked six times: revenue per location rising, renewal rates strong, satisfaction scores above baseline. The committee was about to approve the seventh expansion without a dissenting vote. Camille would later trace the gap to what the model never tracked: not the loyal weekly visitors who generated the revenue signal, but the casual users who had stopped coming without ever registering as a departure.
examples.whatToDo: Before approving the next expansion, run a separate count of inactive accounts from the previous two years. Strong engagement from core users can mask a contracting casual base if the dashboard only measures customers who show up.
examples.whyItMatters: Revenue metrics track the customers who are currently active. They do not track customers who used to be active and are no longer. A shrinking casual base looks like silence on a dashboard built for loyal users.

examples.title: Henrik's Postmortem Explains the Correct Decision

planSpec.domain: taxi dispatch firm renewing a city airport contract on the strength of its enterprise account relationship
planSpec.audience: a dispatch director whose business is defined by its relationship with corporate accounts and hotel concierges
planSpec.stakes: the corporate accounts are delighted and the contract renewal feels secure — but the customers who don't use corporate accounts are not in the room
planSpec.requiredBeat: Henrik explains to the board why the renewal made sense using every metric that mattered inside the current business — and the postmortem shows that all of those metrics were real and all of them described a network that was already shrinking

examples.scenario: The arrivals lane is empty at 11:18 p.m. and has been for forty minutes. Henrik's postmortem for the board is on the table: the contract renewal had been the right decision. Corporate account satisfaction ran at ninety-two percent. Concierge partnership renewals were confirmed. The airport authority had extended on the basis of service metrics no other operator could match. Henrik must now explain to the board why dispatch volume has dropped eighteen percent over the same period that the satisfaction scores were climbing.
examples.whatToDo: Map who is not captured in the corporate account data. The satisfaction metrics describe service to accounts that use the contract. They say nothing about the travelers who used to take taxis before finding a different option.
examples.whyItMatters: A contract built on enterprise accounts measures enterprise account satisfaction accurately. The private passenger who has stopped showing up does not generate a complaint. They simply disappear from the data without registering as a departure.

examples.title: Yusuf Approves the Largest Print Run in a Decade

planSpec.domain: print encyclopedia publisher approving a new edition after a record-breaking sales year
planSpec.audience: an editorial director whose product has just had its strongest year in a decade
planSpec.stakes: a record year makes the investment in a new edition look clearly justified — and makes the threat from digital reference look like a niche problem for librarians, not a mainstream concern
planSpec.requiredBeat: The before shows Yusuf approving the edition based on sales data that is entirely real. The after shows what the sales data could not show: that the customers buying the record year were schools and libraries upgrading aging sets, and that the market that would replace them was forming in a different channel entirely.

examples.scenario: You have just signed off on the largest print run in the company's history. Yusuf's annual review shows record institutional sales driven by school district upgrades, and the pipeline for next year is solid. The before looks like a peak: strong demand, healthy margins, a waiting list for the deluxe edition. The after arrives four years later, when the upgrade cycle ends and the districts that drove the record year are not replacing at the same cadence. The demand was real. It was also the last strong expression of a purchasing pattern that was already shifting.
examples.whatToDo: Identify which customers drove the record and whether their demand is structural or tied to a replacement cycle. A strong year powered by institutional upgrades tells you less about future demand than a strong year driven by first-time buyers.
examples.whyItMatters: Institutional buyers on upgrade cycles can produce strong demand metrics that look like stable market strength. The difference between structural demand and cycle-driven demand is invisible inside a single year of sales data.

questions.prompt: A product line has high satisfaction scores from its top accounts and strong renewal rates. The leadership team uses this data to argue against investing in a simpler, lower-cost version. What is the clearest gap in this reasoning?
choices: The data describes existing buyers accurately but produces no information about potential buyers who find the current product too expensive or too complex to use.
High satisfaction scores are an unreliable indicator of future revenue.
The leadership team should develop the simpler version regardless of what current accounts prefer.
questions.explanation: Current buyer satisfaction data is accurate about current buyers. It cannot describe buyers who are not yet in the system. Using it to reject a product they might adopt is a structural omission, not a measurement error.

questions.prompt: A dispatch company renews a major airport contract after reporting ninety-two percent satisfaction from its corporate accounts. Over the same period, total dispatch volume fell eighteen percent. Which conclusion best explains the gap?
choices: The satisfaction survey used a flawed methodology, and the proper approach would be to separate account-level satisfaction from total service volume trends.

Corporate account satisfaction and total dispatch volume measure different populations: the first captures clients who stayed, while the second reflects trends among all travelers including those who stopped using the service.
A drop in total volume always signals poor service quality regardless of which customer segments are generating the decline.
questions.explanation: A satisfaction metric built on enterprise accounts captures enterprise account satisfaction precisely. It produces no signal from private travelers who stopped using taxis without registering a complaint anywhere in the system.

questions.prompt: A film camera manufacturer surveys two hundred working photographers about a new digital format. Ninety percent say they would not switch from film at current quality levels. What does this finding tell the company, and what does it fail to tell?
choices: The finding confirms that digital cameras have no addressable market among professional or consumer buyers at any price point.
The finding proves the digital format is technically inferior and should be abandoned.
The finding accurately describes the preferences of working photographers but produces no information about buyers who do not currently use professional cameras at all.
questions.explanation: Sampling current professional users confirms what current professional users need. The survey design excludes the buyer who uses a camera occasionally, or not at all, and who might find the digital format's tradeoffs acceptable. That buyer is absent from the data, not absent from the market.

questions.prompt: A franchise chain's highest-revenue locations report that they do not need an online booking platform because their clients call directly. The investment committee votes to shelve the platform based on this feedback. What risk does this create?
choices: The high-revenue franchises are incorrect about their own customers and need independent audits to validate the preferences they reported.
Customer feedback from profitable franchises dominates the committee's signal while the behavior of buyers outside those top locations goes unmeasured.
Online booking platforms are always superior to phone-based booking.
questions.explanation: The feedback from top franchises is accurate about top-franchise customers. The problem is that the committee's dominant signal comes from the locations most committed to the current model, which creates a systematic gap around buyer types those locations do not serve.

questions.prompt: In the disk drive industry, market leaders kept improving their products for current buyers and repeatedly lost position when new disk drive generations emerged. What explains this pattern?
choices: Each generation's leader improved exactly what current buyers needed, which pointed resources away from the smaller-form products that served a different and initially smaller market.
The leaders were cutting corners on quality to reduce manufacturing costs, which caused their loyal enterprise customers to shift purchases to newer entrants.
The new entrants had larger engineering teams and more R&D investment, which let them iterate faster and overtake incumbents who were underinvesting in smaller form factors.
questions.explanation: Sustaining innovations followed the direction current buyers set. That direction was rational and correct for the current market. It was also the direction away from the form factors that later became the mainstream. The investments made sense; the frame they were made inside was narrowing.

questions.prompt: An expansion model has worked reliably across six markets, generating strong revenue per location, renewal rates, and satisfaction scores. The seventh market is approved on the same basis. Which question does the model fail to ask?
choices: Whether the marketing spend is allocated correctly across the new locations.
Whether the satisfaction team is using the right survey instrument.
Whether the customers generating the strong metrics are the core heavy users or a broader casual base that may be contracting separately.
questions.explanation: A dashboard built on active users measures active users well. It cannot distinguish between a stable total market and a market where casual users are drifting away while core users stay strong. The expansion signal is real; the question is what it is actually measuring.

questions.prompt: An editorial director reports record institutional sales for a print reference product, driven by school district upgrade cycles. The investment committee approves a major new edition on this basis. What does the sales record fail to capture?
choices: Whether the school districts will negotiate different pricing next year.
Whether the demand driving the record year is structural market strength or a one-time cycle that will not repeat at the same volume.
Whether the production costs for the new edition are within budget.
questions.explanation: Institutional buyers on replacement cycles can produce peak demand that looks like stable market depth. The upgrade cycle explains the record year. It does not predict what happens when the cohort that just bought completes its cycle.

questions.prompt: A market intelligence director argues that the company is well-protected from competitive threats because it runs the industry's most comprehensive customer satisfaction survey. What is the strongest critique of this position?
choices: Customer satisfaction surveys always overstate loyalty because they only reach respondents who remain active, excluding those who have already left the service.
The director should use net promoter scores instead of satisfaction surveys, which capture both advocates and detractors in the current customer pool more accurately.

A comprehensive survey of current customers produces an accurate picture of the existing market and a blank space where markets not yet served by the company are forming. The comprehensiveness is real; the blind spot is structural.
questions.explanation: The survey is comprehensive within its scope. Its scope is current customers. Buyers who have not yet adopted the category, who find the product too expensive, or who use an alternative that does not appear in the survey simply do not exist in the data. Comprehensive coverage of existing buyers is not comprehensive coverage of the market.

questions.prompt: A product manager concludes that a new technology poses no near-term threat after surveying the top ten accounts and finding that none of them plan to adopt it. Which reasoning error does this commit?
choices: It treats the absence of demand from current top accounts as evidence of no demand from all buyer types, including those not currently in the account base.
It uses account size as the primary filter for evaluating technology threats, which prevents it from detecting adoption patterns among buyers outside the top accounts.
It relies on qualitative feedback rather than quantitative adoption metrics.
questions.explanation: The top accounts are the right people to ask about whether they will adopt the technology. They are not the right people to ask about whether a buyer outside the current account base will adopt it. The survey is correct on its stated population and silent on the next one.

reviewCards.front: Your top accounts just gave you strong feedback that a new product format is not right for them. What should you verify before using that as a reason to kill the project?
reviewCards.back: Check whether the feedback describes the full market or only the current buyer base. Top accounts are telling you the truth about their needs. They cannot tell you what buyers outside their world would accept.

reviewCards.front: A company keeps improving its product for current customers and keeps losing market share to entrants. How is that possible?
reviewCards.back: Improvement follows what current buyers will pay for, which points resources away from the markets entrants can enter first. Serving current buyers well is the mechanism for missing disruptive entrants, not the protection against them.

reviewCards.front: Why was the disk drive industry useful as a research case for studying how great firms fail?
reviewCards.back: Product generations cycled so quickly that the pattern of leadership transfer could be observed in real time rather than over decades. The same mechanism visible elsewhere over a generation played out in years.

reviewCards.front: A company runs strong customer satisfaction scores while total dispatch volume falls. What are the two things being measured differently?
reviewCards.back: Satisfaction scores measure the customers who are still actively using the service. Volume measures all travelers, including those who stopped using the service without registering a complaint. The two populations are not the same.

reviewCards.front: What does 'serving current customers well' prevent a company from seeing?
reviewCards.back: It filters out signal from buyers outside the current value network: buyers who won't pay the same price, don't need the same performance, or use a different channel the company has not built for.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to separate what your current customer feedback can measure from what it cannot, and to treat that gap as a real signal rather than an absence of data.

ifThenPlans.plan: If satisfaction is strong across top accounts, then also pull a count of inactive or lapsed accounts from the same period and ask what those users are doing instead.
If the evaluation team is made up of people serving current customers, then add one explicit question: who would use this at lower quality, and what would they trade away to do so?
If the investment case rests on customer feedback, then identify which buyers are generating that feedback and whether a different type of buyer would reach a different conclusion.
If a competitor is growing in a segment you do not serve, treat their customer base as a signal about what your current measurement instruments cannot reach.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Name one buyer type that has no voice in your most recent product or investment decision. Write one sentence about what that buyer would say about your product if asked today.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Once a week, identify one customer who is not in your measurement system and find out what they use instead of your product. Track that list for a month.

memorableLines.text: What they cannot tell you is where the market is forming that will replace them.
memorableLines.why: Names the structural gap in one sentence without blame or abstraction.

memorableLines.text: The disk drive market was the closest thing to a controlled lab that business research had found: generations turned fast enough that you could watch a leader vanish in real time.
memorableLines.why: Grounds the abstract pattern in a specific empirical case without sounding like a citation.

memorableLines.text: Good management applied to the current business is the mechanism, not the solution.
memorableLines.why: Compresses the chapter's central paradox into a form that is easy to carry and hard to misread.
